title: How Do DPI and a Packet-Based Network Perspective Improve Observability?
summary: NETSCOUT’s deep packet inspection and packet-based insights strengthen observability so teams can resolve application performance problems faster. That same network intelligence gives business leaders clearer answers during incident reviews.
body_markdown:
An insurance claims processing app starts lagging. Complaints are flooding in, overwhelming customer support. The observability team checks dashboards; everything looks fine. The application team spots timeouts; they can’t explain them. Meanwhile, management wants to know when the problem will be fixed.


While everyone is fumbling around in the dark, the answer is right there. On the network.


Observability is traditionally defined as understanding system behavior from its external outputs.[Deep packet inspection (DPI) at scale](https://www.netscout.com/deep-packet-inspection) strengthens[observability](https://www.netscout.com/observability) by extracting insights directly from network traffic. This packet-based perspective helps teams understand why problems occur rather than relying solely on what individual apps report.


NETSCOUT’s[Cisco Live 2026 observability survey](https://www.netscout.com/ebooks/observability-ai-readiness-and-operational-resilience) found that 56.2 percent of surveyed attendees take hours to resolve performance problems, while another 20.8 percent require a day or more. That’s a long time to be searching for answers when[critical applications](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/application-performance-management) are affected.


## What Makes DPI So Important?


The nature of enterprise network traffic is changing rapidly. According to[Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/agentic-web/) , daily requests from AI agents on its network grew more than 1,700 percent over the past year alone. Waiting until something breaks can leave IT teams playing catch-up.


Long recognized for its packet-based approach to network intelligence, NETSCOUT combines DPI at scale, analyzing packets across Layers 2–7, with proprietary Adaptive Service Intelligence (ASI) technology to turn high volumes of network traffic across complex environments into NETSCOUT Smart Data. This semantically rich, protocol-aware metadata reveals interactions and service dependencies directly from the wire, showing how services communicate and perform without requiring teams to manually examine every packet. For[AI workflows](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/aiops-enterprise) , that means more precise operational context[without wasting tokens](https://www.netscout.com/platform) .


Remember that insurance claims app from earlier?


A spike in response times doesn’t tell you whether the problem is in the network or on the server. Packet analysis can expose retransmissions and measure response times to help pinpoint where delays are coming from. That’s the kind of evidence teams need to move beyond debating symptoms.


Now the investigation has somewhere useful to start.


## What Can Packet Analysis Reveal About Application Performance?


The table below shows a few ways a packet-based network perspective can answer common troubleshooting questions.


**The Question** **What the Network Reveals** **Why It Matters**


**Why is an application slow?** Response times, retransmissions, and protocol errors Isolates potential causes of performance issues


**Which services are disrupted?** Communications and dependencies Establishes incident scope


**Which user communities are affected?** Traffic patterns across locations, remote offices, and VPN or VDI users Identifies where problems are concentrated


**Is the network responsible?** Packet loss, retransmissions, and server response times Distinguishes between network and server issues


**What changed?** New connections or unexpected interactions Exposes operational blind spots


**What was the impact?** Transaction failures and service delays Helps assess effects on users, customers, revenue, and reputation


By observing traffic at strategic vantage points on the network, teams can spot problems as they emerge and uncover insights that metrics, events, logs, and traces (MELT) alone may miss.


## Seeing the Evidence Beyond the Alert


Detecting a problem is only the beginning. You also need to understand what caused it and which services are affected.


- **Step 1: Follow the conversations.** Examine communications between clients, critical applications, and supporting services to identify dependencies missing from existing inventories.
- **Step 2: Trace the problem.** Correlate network traffic with application monitoring data to isolate the source.
- **Step 3: Establish the scope.** Identify affected services and combine those findings with operational information, such as support tickets, to assess incident severity.


Together, these steps help teams narrow down the root cause faster.


## When the Questions Reach the Executive Team


Anyone who’s gone through an incident review knows the questions don’t stop when service is restored.


How long was the downtime? Were service-level objectives breached? Did customers lose access? What was the business impact? Could this happen again?


Combined with organizational information, DPI and a packet-based network perspective provide a more detailed view of application interactions to help explain what happened and assess the blast radius. After all, no executive leaves a meeting about an outage wondering about their observability spend. They want answers, especially if the media knows.
